subject: Saiba mais
message: The link text "Saiba mais" does not tell where the link goes, and nothing around it does.

auditor.label: false_positive
auditor.rationale: "Saiba mais" is the button-styled link that closes the home page's "Cidades e Estados" module. It goes to /cidades-e-estados.html?c=4205407, the Cidades e Estados page for the municipality shown. The link sits in the same container as the h2 "Cidades e Estados", which precedes it. In between are the selected city, "Florianópolis ( SC ) - 4205407", and that city's population, area and code (snapshot and screenshot). Under H80, the link text combined with the preceding heading ("Saiba mais" + "Cidades e Estados") describes the purpose: more on this city in Cidades e Estados. That is programmatically determined link context, which is enough for 2.4.4 (Level A). The finding's claim that "nothing around it does" is wrong, and the packet gave the model that heading. Link text on its own would only be required by 2.4.9 (AAA). The live page now shows another capital (Brasília), but the structure is the same.

skeptic.label: false_positive
skeptic.rationale: "Saiba mais" is the button-styled link at the bottom of the "Cidades e Estados" block and points to /cidades-e-estados.html?c=4205407. The finding says nothing around it gives its purpose, and that is wrong. The closest heading before it is the h2 "Cidades e Estados". Between that heading and the link are the place selector showing "Florianópolis ( SC ) - 4205407" and Florianópolis's population, area and municipal code (4205407, the same code as in the href). Under technique H80 (link text plus the preceding heading), "Saiba mais" in the "Cidades e Estados" section identifies the destination: the Cidades e Estados page for the place shown. 2.4.4 accepts programmatically determined context, so this passes even though "Saiba mais sobre Florianópolis" would be clearer. The heading and the block text were in the checker's context (headingsNear, ancestors), so the misjudgement is the model's.

subject: Buscar
message: The placeholder "Buscar" has a contrast of 4.08:1 with the field (#757575 on #f1f1f1). Placeholder text is text, and WCAG 1.4.3 asks for 4.5:1.

auditor.label: true_positive
auditor.rationale: The element is the visible desktop header search field, with placeholder "Buscar". The site CSS sets the field background to #f1f1f1 (input.header__busca--campo), sets no placeholder colour, and uses 16px italic weight 500. That leaves Chrome's default placeholder colour, #757575. Sampling the screenshot inside the field gives a #f1f1f1 background with #757575 glyph cores. The contrast is 4.08:1, which I recomputed. That is below 4.5:1, and the text is not large. The 1.4.3 Understanding document says the criterion covers placeholder text. The field is enabled, so the inactive-component exception does not apply. The placeholder is also the only visible label, because the real label has font-size 0.

skeptic.label: true_positive
skeptic.rationale: This is the header search field's placeholder "Buscar" (16px, weight 500, normal-size text). The darkest glyph pixel in the screenshot is #757575 on a #f1f1f1 field, and live computed styles today give the same rgb(117,117,117) on rgb(241,241,241). That is 4.08:1, below 4.5:1. The placeholder is not incidental: the <label> has font-size:0, so the placeholder and the icon are the only visible cues for the field. The strongest counter-argument is G174: the page has a high-contrast toggle (#setConstrast), and in that mode the placeholder is #757575 on #000, 4.56:1. But the toggle is an <a> with no href. A live Tab test in Edge skips it, going from the logo link straight to the language links, and it is exposed as a generic element rather than a control. A mechanism that only pointer users can reach cannot count as conforming, so the default view's failure stands.

Each label just says "Buscar" (Search), and the patch's claimed label text "Buscar Buscar" does not exist. auditor.label: false_positive
auditor.rationale: The element is the numbered pagination link "2" (href .../acessibilidade-digital/page/2/) in a standard pager shown as "1 2 Próxima página" below the article grid, where "1" is the current page and has aria-current="page". The snapshot and the live page agree (the live HTML is unchanged): the link sits in a list inside <nav aria-labelledby> whose accessible name is "Páginas de Acessibilidade digital". 2.4.4 accepts link text combined with programmatically determined link context, which includes the enclosing list and the labelled navigation landmark. In that context "2" clearly means page 2 of the Acessibilidade digital listing, and the destination's title, "Acessibilidade digital - Página 2 de 2", confirms it. The finding's claim that "nothing around it" gives the purpose is wrong: the nav name was in the context Rampa had (it appears in the packet's ancestors). Requiring the link text alone to state its purpose would be 2.4.9 (AAA), not 2.4.4. "Página 2" would be a nicer label, but its absence is not a 2.4.4 failure.

skeptic.label: false_positive
skeptic.rationale: The element is the "2" link in the archive's pagination: a <nav id="e-pagination" aria-labelledby="lbl-e-pagination"> named "Páginas de Acessibilidade digital" (an sr-only label placed right before the list), holding the list "1" (current page, a span), "2", "Próxima página". The live page still has the same markup. The finding says nothing around the link tells where it goes, and that is wrong: the link sits in a labelled pagination landmark, next to the current page "1" and a "Próxima página" link to the same URL. That context is programmatically determinable (the ancestor nav's accessible name, read out when a screen reader enters the landmark) and also visible, so a user can tell that "2" means page 2 of this listing. The destination, "Acessibilidade digital - Página 2 de 2", is what they would expect. Numbered links in a labelled pagination nav are the standard pattern that auditors accept under 2.4.4 (Level A, in context). Requiring "Página 2" in the link text itself is closer to the stricter 2.4.9 (link only). The checker had the nav name in its ancestors and still judged it wrongly, at low confidence.
